quotes.t: Et si domus pulchra sit, intelligamus eam dominis aedificatam esse, non muribus: sic igitur mundum deorum domum existimare debemus.
quotes.c: We should infer in the case of a beautiful dwelling-place that it was built for its owners and not for mice; we ought, therefore, in the same way to regard the universe as the dwelling-place of the gods. SVF II 1011; Cicero, De Natura Deorum, III.25 (tr. Francis Brooks, 1896)

quotes.t: Ipsumque mundum deum dicit esse et eius animi fusionem universam.
quotes.c: The universe itself is God, or an emanation of the divine mind. SVF II 1077; Cicero, De Natura Deorum, I.39 (tr. Horace C. P. McGregor, 1972)

quotes.t: Qui stadium currit, eniti et contendere debet, quam maxime possit, ut vincat; supplantare eum, quocum certer, aut manu depellere nullo modo debet. Sic in vita sibi quemque petere quod pertineat ad usum, non iniquum est: alteri deripere ius non est.
quotes.c: He who is running a race ought to endeavor and strive to the utmost of his ability to come off victor; but it is utterly wrong for him to trip up his competitor, or to push him aside. So in life it is not unfair for one to seek for himself what may accrue to his benefit; but it is not right to take it from another. SVF III 689; Cicero, De Officiis, III.42 (tr. A. P. Peabody, 1887)

quotes.t: sapientem nulla re egere et tamen multis illi rebus opus esse. contra stulto nulla re opus est, nulla enim re uti scit, sed omnibus eget.
quotes.c: The wise man is in want of nothing, and yet needs many things. On the other hand, nothing is needed by the fool, for he does not understand how to use anything, but he is in want of everything. SVF III 674; Seneca, Moral Epistles, 9.14 (tr. R. M. Gummere, 1918)

quotes.t: εἰ δέ γε ᾔδειν ὅτι νοσεῖν μοι καθείμαρται νῦν, καὶ ὥρμων ἂν ἐπ᾿ αὐτό. καὶ γὰρ ὁ ποῦς, εἰ φρένας εἶχεν, ὥρμα ἂν ἐπὶ τὸ πηλοῦσθαι.
quotes.c: If I knew that it was fated for me to be sick, I would even move toward it; for the foot also, if it had intelligence, would move to go into the mud. SVF III 191; Epictetus, Discourses, II.6.10 (tr. G. Long, 1952)

quotes.t: εἰ τοῖς πολλοῖς προσεῖχον, οὐκ ἂν ἐφιλοσόφησα.
quotes.c: If I had followed the multitude, I should not have studied philosophy. SVF II 10; Diogenes Laërtius, VII.182 (tr. R. D. Hicks, 1925)

quotes.t: ἴσον ἐστὶ τὸ κατ᾿ ἀρετὴν ζῆν τῷ κατ᾿ ἐμπειρίαν τῶν φύσει συμβαινόντων ζῆν.
quotes.c: Living virtuously is equivalent to living in accordance with experience of the actual course of nature. SVF III 4; Diogenes Laërtius, VII.87 (tr. R. D. Hicks, 1925)

quotes.t: The end of life is happiness, and happiness is achieved by living virtuously.
The end of life is to live in accordance with reason, and the perfection of human nature is to live virtuously.
The end of man is action, and not mere speculation.
The good is what is useful for the soul, the bad is what is harmful to the soul.
The good or happy life is produced by noble actions; it is not by chance.
The soul is a blend of fire and air.
The soul is a blend of the four elements.
The soul is a body that is capable of movement and sensation.
The soul is a harmony of the body.
The soul is a harmony of the elements.
The soul is the principle of sensation, and the body is the instrument of sensation.
The soul is the self-moving pneuma, or vital spirit.
The universe is a unity, a single whole, which is governed by a single law.
The wise man is always at ease, for he is never disturbed by external circumstances.
The wise man is always cheerful, for he is never out of tune with Nature.
The wise man is always prepared, for he has provided himself with everything he needs.
The wise man is free, for he is not subject to external circumstances.
The wise man is he who, in the midst of business and confusion, is still and calm at heart.
